pages.text: The notice was on the board by the estate management office on a Tuesday. It said: In response to increased demand for vehicle parking, the structure commonly known as the Old Hut, located at the south-east corner of the estate gardens, will be demolished on the 15th of this month to allow for the construction of an additional six parking spaces. The management committee thanks residents for their understanding.

image.note: Illustration: a printed notice on a board, three children reading it with increasingly alarmed expressions

pages.text: Emeka read it twice, which was his habit with any official document, to make sure he had understood it correctly and not simply had a strong reaction to the wrong thing. He had understood it correctly. He had a strong reaction to the correct thing.

Isa photographed the notice with his phone. 'Evidence,' he said. 'Of what?' Kemi said. 'Of what they are proposing to do,' Isa said. 'The notice is right there,' Kemi said. 'I have read it. Isa has read it. You have read it.' 'This is a physical copy of the evidence,' Isa said. He did not appear to see a problem.

The old hut was on the south-east corner of the estate gardens, near the hedge, and had been there longer than anyone currently living on the estate could clearly remember. It was made of concrete and had a tin roof that hummed in the rain. It had a door that did not lock but also did not blow open in the wind, which meant it had been hung at exactly the right angle. The estate children used it as a base, a meeting point, a shelter in sudden rain, and a place to leave things that were too large to carry home.

image.note: Illustration: the gazebo/hut from outside, children visible through the open door sitting on the low wall

pages.text: 'The question,' Emeka said, 'is what argument we can make to the management committee that they have not already considered.' He had written this at the top of the page in his notebook and underlined it. 'They want six parking spaces,' he continued. 'We want the hut. The question is whether we have a reason that outweighs six parking spaces.'
'It is the best hut on the estate,' Kemi said. 'There is only one hut on the estate,' Isa said. 'It is still the best one,' Kemi said.
Emeka's pen did not move. 'We need a reason that works for the committee,' he said. 'Not a reason that works for us. Those are different audiences.'

The hut did not look like much, and that was rather the point of it. It was a squat concrete box with a tin roof, a door that hung at an angle that only looked wrong until you tried it, and a smell, when it rained, of warm dust and old paint. Grown-ups walked past it without a glance. To the estate children it was the single most important building on the whole estate, because it was theirs in a way that nothing else was.

It was where you went when the rain came suddenly. It was where you left the football too big to carry home. It was where a plan was made, a secret kept, a quarrel settled. None of that was written on any notice or recorded in any office, which was exactly why the management could schedule its demolition without a second thought. You cannot put on a form the value of a place where children have been allowed, for once, to be simply left alone.

The estate manager was a precise man called Mr Obi who wore pressed trousers even on weekends and who had been managing the estate since it was built. He had agreed to a ten-minute meeting because Emeka had written him a letter. The letter had one specific question in it: was the old hut part of the original 1987 construction? Emeka had found the founding year on the estate information board in the lobby, which listed it in small print at the bottom. He had gone back twice to make sure he had read it correctly.

image.note: Illustration: Mr Obi behind a desk, four children in chairs opposite, Emeka's letter visible on the desk

pages.text: 'Yes,' Mr Obi said, without needing to check anything. 'It was the original security post. Built when the estate was first constructed. The gate security officer used it before the current gatehouse was built in 2003.' He said this with the tone of someone reciting a fact he had always known but had never been asked. 'So it is the oldest structure on the estate,' Emeka said. It was not quite a question. 'Yes,' Mr Obi said. He seemed, very slightly, to be thinking about this in a new way.

'If you demolish it,' Isa said, 'you will be demolishing the oldest structure on the estate.' He had prepared this sentence in advance. It landed with more weight than he had expected. 'That is accurate,' Mr Obi said, slowly.

Kemi, who had been quiet for eleven minutes, said: 'Can we put a sign on it?' Everyone looked at her. 'A sign. Saying what it is. If people know it is the oldest building on the estate, they will think differently about parking on top of it.' She looked at Emeka. 'That is the audience argument, isn't it? That is the one you wanted.'

The management committee met the following week. Mr Obi presented the historical case for the hut and a counter-proposal: the six parking spaces would be accommodated by removing a section of the largely unused overflow path on the north side of the estate instead. The hut would receive a small metal plaque identifying it as the original estate security post, established 1987.

image.note: Illustration: four children watching as an estate worker screws a small plaque to the wall of the hut

pages.text: The plaque was slightly crooked on the first attempt. The worker straightened it. Emeka watched the straightening with the focused attention he gave to all calibration activities. When it was level, he nodded once.

'It doesn't look different,' Kemi said, looking at the hut. 'It looks exactly like it did before.' 'It is different,' Isa said, pointing at the plaque. 'It has an official status now. It has been documented.' 'It was always the oldest building on the estate,' Kemi said. 'Yes,' Isa said. 'Now it is officially the oldest building on the estate. Those are different things.' Kemi thought about this. It was possible he was right.

That afternoon it rained suddenly, as afternoon rain sometimes arrives with very little warning. Three children ran to the hut. It was not the cleanest shelter. The roof hummed. The door swung at exactly the right angle. Outside, the rain fell on the new plaque and on the old concrete wall and on six parking spaces that did not exist, and the estate was exactly as it had always been, which was, the children agreed, the point.

The plaque, when it was finally fixed to the wall, was smaller than Kemi had imagined and shinier. It caught the afternoon light and threw it back, and the estate worker stepped away, tilted his head, and screwed it a quarter turn straighter without being asked, which Emeka appreciated more than he said. Original Estate Security Post, it read. Established 1987. Eight words. It had taken a letter, a meeting, a history lesson, and a good deal of nerve to earn those eight words.

Nothing about the hut looked different. The door still hung at its angle. The roof still hummed in the rain. But something had changed all the same, and it was this: the hut was now known. It had a past that was written down, a name that was official, a claim on the estate's memory that no parking plan could simply erase. Kemi thought about that as the first fat drops of an afternoon storm began to fall, and the children, as they always had, ran for the door.
